             Studies on Lophocoleaceae. XIX. The systematic identity of
             Cyanolophocolea R.M. Schust., an intriguing liverwort from
              New Zealand and Australia, based on morphological and
                                molecular evidence

                                                  John J. Engel1,3 and Xiaolan He2

               1
                 Department of Botany, Field Museum, Chicago, IL 60605-2496, U.S.A.; 2 Botanical
                Museum, Finnish Museum of Natural History, University of Helsinki, P.O. Box 7,
                                         FIN-00014, Helsinki, Finland

               ABSTRACT. Cyanolophocolea echinella R.M.Schust. is an intriguing species, possessing some
               character states characteristic of the genus Chiloscyphus, such as the ability to produce both male
               and female gametangia on leading shoots, while having other features that are generic characters of
               Heteroscyphus, namely presence of gametangia on short, abbreviated lateral-intercalary branches.
               Its systematic identity was here studied using morphological and DNA sequence data of the
               chloroplast gene regions of rbcL, rps4 and trnL-F. Thirty-seven exemplars including eight of
               Cyanolophocolea echinella, 27 of Lophocoleaceae and two of Plagiochilaceae were used for
               phylogenetic reconstruction using both maximum parsimony and Bayesian inference methods.
               Our analyses placed Cyanolophocolea echinella within Heteroscyphus with strong support.
               Heteroscyphus echinellus (Lindenb. & Gottsche) J.J.Engel & XiaoL.He is proposed and based on
               morphological variations two varieties, var. echinellus and var. hyalinus J.J.Engel, are recognized. A
               large indel (59 base pairs) and one substitution in the trnL intron region, and also one substitution
               in the intergenic spacer region were found in the trnL-F in two Cyanolophocolea echinella
               exemplars both with hyaline oil-bodies. This indicates rapid molecular evolution might have
               occurred within the species.

               KEYWORDS. Chiloscyphus, Cyanolophocolea, Heteroscyphus, Marchantiophyta, rbcL, rps4, trnL-F,
               phylogeny, taxonomy.

4.5.2 Corticolous bryophytes on Athrotaxis             selagilloideslA. taxi/olia.
lbirteen trees of Athrotaxis selaginoides and two trees of A. [axifolia were sampled
throughout the study sites. A total of 2 1 bryophytes were recorded on the trunk of
these softwood species. which are given in Table 4.5. On this phorophyte the ratio of
hepatic to moss was 6 : 1 , with 1 8 hepatic species and only three moss species. All
these mosses and 12 of the hepatic species were also found on Notho/agus
cunninghamii.



The variation in distribution of moss and hepatic species on the 1 5 trees sampled is
given in Fig 4.3. Every tree sampled supported at least one hepatic epiphyte, the
greatest number (10) occurred on only one tree. Moss epiphytes were rare on this
phorophyte with five trees supporting no species and only a single species on the
remaining 16 trees. The only moss which was frequently found on the trunk of
Athrotaxis was Rhizogonium novae-hol/andiae. The hepatics which occurred with

the greatest frequency were; Bazzania involuta, Lepidozia ulothrix, Acromastigum
mooreanum,      Heteroscyphus     cymbaliferus,   Plagiochila    circinalis,   Bazzania

monilinervis, Acromastigum sp. and Lepidozia sp.

4.5.3 Key Taxa
The bryophyte species which had a frequency of occurrence of 25% or more on either
phorophyte are arbitrarily considered to be key epiphyte species. For the mosses they
included; Dicranoloma      mem.iesii,    Hypnum     chrysogaster.     Wijkia    extenuata,
LeplOrileca gaudichaudii. Rhizogonium novae-hollandiae and Dicranoloma robuslLlm
var. selosum. For the bepatics (hey included; Ba72llnia lnvaluta, Gackstroemia
weindoiferi. Acrochila biserialis. Bazzania        monilinervis,    Lepidozia    ulothrix,
Lepidozia sp., ParaschislOchi/a lu/aides, Acromasligum mooreanum, Acromasligum
sp., Heteroscyphus cymbaliferus and Plagiochila circinalis . All the above moss
species are found on similar substrate in New Zealand and south-eastern mainland
Australia. The above hepatic species are found on similar substrate in New Zealand
but in Australia, P. tuloides, A. mooreanum and H. cymbaliferus are confined to
Tasmania.


The following descriptions provide the diagnostic features to allow the identification
of the key moss and hepatic epiphytes that occur on N. cunninghamii and Athrotaxis,
as well as their distinguishing characters from related species. It is not intended to be
a taxonomic account for each species since that is already available in the published
literature.


Dicranoloma menziesii (TayL) Par.
This species is one of the more distinctive for the genus. As an epiphyte jt forms
loose, open dark-green cushions. The leaves are very long and slender and it may be
distinguished vegetatively from other species in the genus by the more or less
isodiametric cells in the upper part of the lamina (Fig 4.6). When fruiting there is a
short seta and the capsules are therefore overtopped by the leaves.
It is mainly confined to the basal region of the trunk and in the sites sampled was only
found on Nothofagus cunninghamii.


Dicranoloma robustum (Hook. f. & Wils.) Par. var. setosum
This taxon is a yellow-brown colour and is readily distinguished from the preceeding
species by the fragile leaves, which have the upper part broken off to give the cushion
a neat spiky appearance. If this feature is not apparent tben the lamina cells are thick­
walled, porose and elongate (Fig. 4.6) thereby providing a marked difference to the
former species.
This taxon is found higher up the trunk of Nothofagus cunninghamii to which it was

Paraschistochila tuloides (Hook. f. Tayl.) Schust.
The flattened shoots of this species, which are rarely branched, are tighdy pressed to

the bark. There are no uoderleaves and the lateral leaves have a dorsal lobe which

produces a keel to the leaf. The only other epiphytic species,       P. pinnatifolia, is
golden-green in colour and is distinguished by having stems branched dichotomously

with the tip of the shoot curved downwards. P. tuloides was found only on the trunk

of N. cllnninghamii throughout the study sites.



Heteroscyphus cymbaliferus (Hook. f. Tayl.) Engel & Schust.
The stems of this species have close imbricate leaves which form compact pale­

yellow clumps. The distinctive character is that the anterior margin of the leaf has a

saccate lobe and the broad underleaf also possesses a saccate lobe at either end.

The species was more frequently found on Athrotaxis and rare on N. cunninghamii.



Plagiochila circinalis (Lehm.) Lehm. & Lindenb.
The brownish shoots of this species are ascending and commonly curve downwards

at the tip. The leaves are closely imbricate, almost circular with a few large teeth and

the ventral margin is somewhat undulate. The leaf cells throughout are very

distinctive with extremely thick trigonous walls.

This species was found on the trunk of N. cunninghamii and Athrotaxis.

of circumferential line transects, every 20cm from the interface of the trunk. with the
buttress up to a height of 2 metres. The sampling points on each transect were 20cm
apart and the species of epiphyte present at each point was recorded.


The percentage bryophyte cover by all species up to a height of 2m on               N.
cunninghamii is given in Fig 4.10. Apart from the basal region of the trunk, the
bryophyte cover is not markedly different on the trunk of N. cunninghamii in the
contrasting rainforest communities. An analysis of the bryophyte cover in terms of
hepatic:moss ratio reveals that the hepatics are the dominant group of bryophytes.
Furthermore, this trend in the dominance of hepatics as the epiphytic cover on the
trunk of N. cunninghamii is consistent in both callidendrous and implicate rainforest
communities (Fig 4. 1 1).


The difference in the bryophyte cover between the rainforest communities lies in the
species composition, especially the hepatics. Table 4.6 provides a list of the moss and
hepatic species that were measured on the trunks of N. cunninghamii. There were
seven moss species in the callidendrous forest and this was reduced to three in the
implicate forest. The only common species was Hypnum chrysogaster. Ten hepatic
species were measured in callidendrous rainforest which increased to 1 5 on the trunk
of N. cunninghamii in implicate rainforest. The common species were Bauania
involuta, Lepidozia ulothrix, Acrochila biserialis, Paraschistochila tilloides and P.
pinnatifolia. Of these B. involuta would appear to be an jmportant indicator species.
The percentage cover of this species to the total hepatic cover in both callidendrous
and implicate rainforest is provided in Fig 4.12. It dominates the hepatic composition
in callidendrous rainforest and shows a gradual reduction in cover with the height of
the trunk. In implicate rainforest, B. involuta   is a markedly reduced component
compared to the other hepalic species and tends to only occupy the basal region of the
trunk of the host tree. IL is replaced by a mixrure of other hepatic species, in
particular,   Heteroscyphus    cymbaliferus,   Lepicolea    scolopendra,    Herberrus
oldfieldianus and Acrochila biserialis.

LEPTOSCYPHUS_2010  (1) 
Abstract A revised classification of the liverwort genus Leptoscyphus (Lophocoleaceae) is presented on the basis of previous
      phylogenetic analyses as well as morphological examination of recent plant material and type specimens. The three subgenera
      that have traditionally been recognized based on morphological grounds, namely Leptoscyphus subg. Anomylia, L. subg. Phy-
      soscyphus, and L. subg. Leptoscyphus, are well retrieved by the phylogeny. Two new subgenera, L. subg. Spinoscyphus and L.
      subg. Australoleptoscyphus, are created for L. cleefii and L. spectabilis and the southern South Hemisphere species, respectively.
      Three new species, namely L. gradsteinii, L. lambinonii, and L. sotiauxii, are described here based on molecular and morpho-
      logical evidence. The new combination L. porphyrius subsp. azoricus is made. Lectotypes are designated for Chiloscyphus
      australis, C. huidobroanus, Jungermannia amphibolia, J. pallidovirens, J. physocalyx, Lophocolea belmorana, L. diversifolia,
      L. excipulata, and Mylia azorica.

      Keywords lectotype; Leptoscyphus; liverworts

et al., 2007c). Instead of reducing all of these genera to Chiloscyphus, well-supported
                 monophyletic lineages that have been recognised as subgenera by Hentschel et al.
                 (2007c) can be recognised as genera. The fairly large clade that includes Lophocolea
                 bidentata (L.) Dumort. (5 Chiloscyphus latifolius (Nees) J.J.Engel & R.M.Schust.),
                 the type species of Lophocolea, excludes the type species of Chiloscyphus, and is
                 herein recognised as comprising the genus Lophocolea. Campanocolea (accommo-
                 dating Lophocolea fragmentissima R.M.Schust.) is nested in this clade and is
                 justifiably reduced to Lophocolea. Like Lophocolea, Leptoscyphus is strongly
                 supported as a monophyletic lineage that can be recognised as a genus. Evidence
                 for the reduction of Pachyglossa to Chiloscyphus (Hentschel et al., 2007c) is weak,
                 with only 65% bootstrap support in maximum likelihood analysis for its resolution
                 as a sister taxon to Chiloscyphus subgen. Notholophocolea and we therefore continue
                 to recognise this genus. The reduction of Invisocaulis to Pachyglossa is based on the
                 morphological studies of Váňa & Gremmen (2005). Species of Clasmatocolea are
                 resolved in three lineages, suggesting that this problematic genus is in need of further
                 study before decisions regarding its status are made. Indeed, rather than reducing
                 many genera to Chiloscyphus, the problem of its paraphyly could be solved by
                 revising the genus to exclude those elements that are not resolved in the lineage of the

                      Dinckleria replacing Proskauera (Engel & Heinrichs, 2008). According to Groth
                      (2005), the placement of Acrochila in the family is equivocal, with rps4 data placing it
                      with Plagiochilaceae, but rbcL data placing it with Jamesoniellaceae. Pedinophyllum
                      appears to be paraphyletic, with P. truncatum (Steph.) Inoue from Japan nested in
                      the Jamesoniellaceae and P. interruptum (Nees) Kaal., which is the type species of
                      Pedinophyllum, resolved in the Plagiochilaceae (Groth, 2005). Although He-Nygrén
                      et al. (2006) included only Pedinophyllum truncatum in their studies, they concluded
                      that Pedinophyllum is an element of the Jamesoniellaceae. It is notable that these two
                      elements, which were once considered subspecies of a single species (Inoue, 1958),
                      have been consistently resolved in two different suborders. It is possible that the
                      single accession of Pedinophyllum truncatum that provided the sequences used by all
                      authors (e.g. Groth, 2005; Heinrichs et al., 2005; He-Nygrén et al., 2006; Hentschel
                      et al., 2007b) was misidentified and actually is Jamesoniella, but Groth (2005) has
                      indicated that an additional unpublished sequence of P. truncatum also places it in
                      the Jamesoniellaceae. Such findings definitely underscore the importance of including
                      the type species in molecular studies before translating the resultant phylogeny into
                      a classification scheme.
                         The unexpected placement of Jamesoniellaceae, once considered a subfamily of
                      Jungermanniaceae (e.g. Crandall-Stotler & Stotler, 2000; Schuster, 2002), in the
                      Cephaloziineae has been confirmed in several studies (e.g. He-Nygrén et al., 2006; De
                      Roo et al., 2007; Hentschel et al., 2007b). Genera currently included in the family
                      follow Schuster’s interpretation of the subfamily, as delineated in 2002. This includes
                      Roivainenia, which Schuster (2002) initially placed in Jungermanniaceae subfam.
                      Lophozioideae, but on review, transferred to the subfamily Jamesonielloideae based
                      on similarities in gynoecial structure (Schuster, 2002: 345). Unpublished molecular
                      data (J. Shaw et al.) further support this transfer. Groth & Heinrichs (2005) sug-

                                              iii
Abstract




Before this study the known Lord Howe Island bryophyte flora (mosses, liverworts and
hornworts) totalled 173 species, consisting of 131 mosses, 40 liverworts and 2 hornworts.

For this study I conducted one month of field studies on the island, during which I collected
more than 650 specimens, and also studied collections from the island held in Australian
herbaria and other collections available in overseas herbaria.

Fourteen moss, 32 liverwort and 1 hornwort species are newly reported from Lord Howe Island,
including one liverwort new to science. A further 2 moss and 2 liverwort varieties are also new
to the island. Twenty-eight moss and 11 liverwort species are discounted from the island’s flora,
as well as 3 moss varieties and 1 liverwort variety. As a result, the known bryophyte flora now
totals 178 species, consisting of 117 moss species (122 taxa), 58 liverwort species (60 taxa) and
3 hornwort species. These totals exclude 5 moss and 2 liverwort species whose taxonomic status
or presence on the island is considered uncertain. One liverwort variety, Heteroscyphus
echinellus var. echinellus, is new to Australia.

Fourteen bryophyte species and one variety are endemic to the island. Spiridens muelleri,
previously thought to be the same as S. vieillardii from New Caledonia, is shown to be a
separate species endemic to Lord Howe Island. Chiloscyphus howeanus is also shown to be a
legitimate species endemic to the island. Cololejeunea elizabethae is described as a new species,
also endemic to the island. Trachyloma wattsii, considered to be endemic to Lord Howe Island,
is supported by a molecular analysis as a legitimate species most closely allied to T. planifolium.

Confusion about the correct identities of the two Ptychomitrium species on the island is resolved
through a revision of the genus for Australia. A previously unrecorded morphological character
of Atrichum androgynum is described from a study of Lord Howe Island plants, and a molecular
analysis shows that South American plants previously ascribed to A. androgynum do not belong
to that species. Hypnodendron vitiense is shown to be paraphyletic, but not as circumscribed by
Touw (1971). The Lord Howe Island plants appear to belong to a morphologically cryptic
species distinct from H. vitiense s.str, and substantial genetic variation within H. vitiense subsp.
australe as currently circumscribed suggests that it might include more than one taxon.

Other molecular investigations clarify the relationship between Lord Howe Island populations
and mainland Australian populations of a number of moss species.

An original and novel investigation of the potential modes of transport of bryophyte propagules
to and from the island is made, and a hypothesis is formed about the origins of its bryophyte
flora and the biogeographic relationships to the Australian land mass and other western Pacific

                                                   iv
islands, including New Zealand and New Caledonia. The nearest region of the Australian
mainland is shown to be the most likely origin of most of the island’s bryoflora, with the
injection of propagules into the high-level jet stream by storms the most likely dispersal
mechanism. The presence of numerous otherwise tropical species on the island is probably a

3          Polytrichales
Polytrichaceae Schwägr. in Willd.
The family Polytrichaceae is generally characterised by the presence of wall-like lamellae of
stacked cells running longitudinally along the adaxial side of the leaf lamina, and by the

---

family, containing at least 25 genera and over 200 species. Two genera occur on Lord Howe
Island.

Geocalyx Nees
Seven extant species are attributed to this genus, but it has not been monographed and I think,
from my reading of the original descriptions, that some species are synonymous or belong to
other genera. Scott (1985) already noted that G. novae-zelandiae is a synonym of
G. caledonicus.

Geocalyx caledonicus Steph.
Geocalyx caledonicus Steph., Sp. Hepat. 3: 265 (1908)
Type: NEW CALEDONIA: Balansa s.n., without date, G not seen.
Description: This species has been described by Allison and Child (1975) and Scott (1985).
Illustration: Also Scott (1985, Figure 78).
Habitat: Rotting wood.
Distribution on LHI: Known only from the eastern slopes of Mt Lidgbird.

                                                 220
Total distribution: Australia (Tas to tropical Qld), New Caledonia, New Zealand.
Discussion: This species has not been reported previously from Lord Howe Island, possibly
because its two locations there are difficult to reach. Its presence on the island is not surprising,
since it is known from New Caledonia, eastern Australia and New Zealand. Scott (1985) stated
that the oil bodies take up much of the cell area, which might give the impression that they
dominate the cell. However, in the Lord Howe Island material at least, the oil bodies rarely take
up more than half of the cell area in plane view.
Unlike its Northern Hemisphere congener Geocalyx graveolens (Schrad.) Nees, which is called
Turpswort in Britain on account of its pungent odour when crushed fresh (Atherton et al. 2010),
G. caledonicus has no odour.

Heteroscyphus Schiffn.
The genus Heteroscyphus has not been monographed, and the only general treatment available
for Australia is that of Scott (1985), and then only for southern Australia. Despite this, the three
species known from Lord Howe Island are readily identified and differentiated, as follows:

Key to Heteroscyphus for Lord Howe Island
1   Leaf  and  stem  surfaces  covered  in  spine-­‐like  papillae  ..............................................................  echinellus  
     Leaf  and  stem  surfaces  smooth  ..............................................................................................................  2  
2   Underleaves  kidney-­‐shaped,  2–3  times  the  width  of  the  stem,  toothed  
    and  incised  all  around  the  margin    ...........................................................................................  fissistipus  
     Underleaves  not  kidney-­‐shaped,  less  than  twice  the  width  of  the  stem,  
     deeply  bifid  with  only  1  or  2  accessory  teeth  on  each  side  .........................................................  argutus  

Heteroscyphus argutus (Reinw., Blume & Nees) Schiffn.
Jungermannia arguta Reinw., Blume & Nees, Nova Acta Phys.-Med. Acad. Caes. Leop.-Carol. Nat.
Curios. 12: 206 (1824); Chiloscyphus argutus (Reinw., Blume & Nees) Nees, in Gottsche, Lindenberg &
Nees, Syn. Hepat. 2: 183 (1845); Heteroscyphus argutus (Reinw., Blume & Nees) Schiffn, Oesterr. Bot.
Zeit. 60: 172 (1910)
Type: INDONESIA: MacCluer-Bai [= MacCluer Gulf, West Papua], Naumann s.n. 1875, not
seen.
Description: For detailed descriptions of this species see Scott (1985) and Piippo (1985).
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figure 83), Piippo (1985, Figure 4k–m).
Habitat: Soil, bark, rotting wood or rarely rock in damp to wet situations; rarely semi-aquatic.
Distribution on LHI: Upland forests, usually close to water; occasionally immersed or semi-
immersed in water.
Total distribution: Australia (eastern Victoria to northern Queensland, Lord Howe I, Norfolk
I.), Malesia, islands of the western Pacific.
Discussion: One specimen (Meagher LH-455) of this species was made from a thriving
population floating freely in a pool in Erskine Creek. As far as I know, this ability to grow and
thrive as an aquatic species has not been reported previously.
Heteroscyphus argutus is a largely tropical species, but in Australia its range extends the
temperate south-east, as far south as Wilsons Promontory in Victoria (Scott 1985). Schiffner
(1900) noted that the species is rather variable in gametophyte characters, and described six
varieties in addition to the ‘forma typica’ (see key below). However, the range of variation of


                                                                          221
the species has never been thoroughly investigated, and it may be that more than one species is
involved.
The following key is based on the Latin descriptions given by Schiffner (1900). On this basis
the Lord Howe Island plants would belong to var. argutus, but as it is uncertain whether
Schiffner’s varieties involve more than one species, and he did not treat any of the six varieties
described by Gottsche et al. (1847) (as var. β, γ, etc.), I have not identified the plants below
species level. None of the other varieties have been formally transferred to Heteroscyphus.
Herzog and Noguchi (1955) failed to cite the basionym when transferring var. brevidens to
Heteroscyphus, so their transfer is illegitimate.

Key to the varieties of Heteroscyphus argutus sensu Schiffner (1900)
1   Underleaves  4-­‐fid  but  armed  with  accessory  teeth  or  cilia;  leaf  with  6–10  
    marginal  teeth  .................................................................................................................  var.  ciliatistipus  
     Underleaves  simply  4-­‐fid,  lacking  accessory  teeth  or  cilia;  number  of  
     marginal  teeth  on  leaves  various  ............................................................................................................  2  
2   Plants  25–30  mm  long  and  up  to  1.5  mm  wide  ......................................................................................  3  
     Plants  30–40  mm  long  and  wider  than  1.5  mm  (usually  much  wider)  ...................................................  4  
3   Leaves  with  2–4  very  short  teeth,  1–2  cells  long  ...............................................................  var.  brevidens  
     Leaves  with  5–6  teeth,  2–3cells  long  .......................................................................................  var.  minor  
4   Leaves  with  2–5  teeth  .............................................................................................................................  5  
     Leaves  with  6  or  more  teeth  ...................................................................................................................  6  
5   Sinuses  between  teeth  deep  and  rounded;  leaf  apex  ±  as  wide  as  base;  3–
    4  strong,  irregular  teeth  ..........................................................................................................  var.  excisus  
     Sinus  between  teeth  shallow,  ±  V-­‐shaped;  leaf  apex  narrower  than  base;  
     2–5  ±  regular  teeth  .....................................................................................................  var.  paucidentatus  
6   Leaves  (at  least  at  the  base)  wider  than  long;  teeth  long,  ±  7  in  number  ...................  var.  subquadratus  
     Leaves  as  long  or  longer  than  wide;  teeth  short  (2–3  cells),  or  if  long  then  
     up  to  11  in  number  .................................................................................................................................  7  
7   Leaves  with  6–11  teeth  ..........................................................................................................  var.  argutus  
     Leaves  with  5–6  teeth  ..............................................................................................................  var.  minor  



Heteroscyphus allodontus (Hook.f. & Taylor) J.J.Engel & R.M.Schust. was reported from Lord
Howe Island by Stephani and Watts (1914) on the basis of a collection by Watts (Watts LHI
76b, NSW-818150). Unfortunately this collection could not be found during this study.
However, it is notable that there are no collections by Watts of Heteroscyphus argutus from the
island, despite it being very common in Erskine Valley where Watts 76b was collected. Poorly
developed specimens of H. argutus are quite common among collections from Lord Howe
Island, often bearing only two or three teeth at the apex and with the underleaf armature
reduced. It is possible that Watts 76b is merely such a weak form of that species, equivalent to
Schiffner’s variety paucidentatus.
It is noteworthy that the type, from the Auckland Islands, was growing on the bark of trees
(Taylor and Hooker 1845), which is a very unusual habitat for Geocalycaceae generally, and
that the species has never been fully described or illustrated, so that the identification of the
numerous specimens in New Zealand herbaria (AVH 2018) must be considered tentative.
At present I prefer to consider Heteroscyphus allodontus as ‘uncertain’ for Lord Howe Island,
pending an assessment of Watts 76b when it is found.



                                                                              222
Heteroscyphus echinellus (Lindenb. and Gottsche) J.J.Engel and X.L.He var.
echinellus
Lophocolea echinella Lindenb. & Gottsche, in Gottsche, Lindenberg & Nees, Syn. Hepat. 5: 703 (1847);
Chiloscyphus echinellus (Lindenb. & Gottsche) Mitt., in Hooker, Fl. Nov.-Zel. 2(2): 141 (1854);
Cyanolophocolea echinella (Lindenb. & Gottsche) R.M.Schust., Nova Hedwigia 72: 102 (2001);
Heteroscyphus echinellus (Lindenb. & Gottsche) J.J.Engel & X.L.He, Bryologist 113: 115 (2010)
Description: This species was comprehensively described by Engel and He (2010).
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figure 84, 85), Engel and He (2010, Figures 3–5).
Habitat: Soil, bark and rotting wood in damp to wet situations.
Distribution on LHI: Summit Plateau of Mt Gower, on rotting wood in very wet situations in
deep gullies.
Total distribution: Eastern Australia (Tasmania to southern Queensland, Lord Howe I.), New
Zealand.
Discussion: Heteroscyphus echinellus was previously known only from New Zealand,
Tasmania and Victoria (Engel and He 2010). Lord Howe Island is thus the mostly northerly
known point of its distribution. The variety echinellus was thought to have been endemic to
New Zealand, with only H. echinellus var. hyalinus J.J.Engel known from Australia (Engel and
He 2010). This variety is therefore new to the Australian flora. It is easily distinguished from
var. hyalinus even in the field because it has plane rather than downcurved leaf apices, so that
the spinose armature around the apex is clearly visible in dorsal view (Engel and He 2010).

Heteroscyphus fissistipus (Hook.f. & Taylor) Schiffn, Oesterr. Bot. Zeit. 60: 172
(1910)
Jungermannia fissistipa Hook.f. & Taylor, London J. Bot. 3: 384 (1844)
Chiloscyphus fissistipus (Hook.f. & Taylor) Taylor ex Gottsche, Lindenb. & Nees, Syn. Hepat. 2: 175
(1845)
Type: NEW ZEALAND: Auckland Islands, J.D. Hooker s.n., date unknown, herb. Taylor, not
seen.
Description: Scott (1985) published a general description of this species that is adequate for
identification.
Illustrations: Figure 3. Also Scott (1985, Figure 85), Meagher and Fuhrer (2003, pages 264–
265).
Habitat: Soil, bark and rotting wood in damp to wet situations.
Distribution on LHI: Eastern slopes of Mt Lidgbird, Erskine Valley.
Total distribution: Eastern Australia (Tasmania to southern Queensland, Lord Howe I.), New
Zealand.
Discussion: Heteroscyphus fissistipus is one of the most common species of Heteroscyphus in
southern Australia, from Tasmania to southern Queensland. Stephani and Watts (1914) reported
Chiloscyphus multifidus Steph. from Lord Howe Island on the basis of a collection by W.W.
Watts (presumably Watts LHI 88, NSW-818174). This specimen was not available during the
present study. However, C. multifidus appears to be conspecific with H. fissistipus judging by
Stephani’s original description (Stephani 1906–1909: 132) and his sketch in the Icones
(Stephani 1985) drawn from the type. It is notable that only one other collection identified as
C. multifidus exists in Australian and New Zealand herbaria (Clark s.n., MEL-64300A), and is
no different from H. fissistipus as circumscribed by Scott (1985).

                                                  223
Until Watts LHI 88 can be studied or the status of Heteroscyphus multifidus is clarified, I prefer
to treat the species as ‘uncertain’ in the Lord Howe Island flora.


Balantiopsaceae H.Buch
Balantiopsis Mitt.
Balantiopsis is a largely south temperate genus, although extending into the tropics from
Malesia to Brazil. The genus was monographed by Engel (1968), who recognised 13 species.
Since then another three species have been recognised. Three species are known from Australia.
One species occurs on Lord Howe Island.

Balantiopsis diplophylla (Hook.f. & Taylor) Mitt.
Jungermannia diplophylla Hook.f. & Taylor, London J. Bot. 3: 377 (1844); Gottschea diplophylla
(Hook.f. & Taylor) Nees, Syn. Hepat. 624 (1846); Balantiopsis diplophylla (Hook.f. & Taylor) Mitt.,
Rep. Challenger Bot. 1(3): 87 (1855)
Type: NEW ZEALAND, J.D. Hooker s.n., Auckland Islands, 1841, holotype unknown;
isotypes E-2028!d, E-28028!d
Description: This species was fully described by Engel (1968).
Illustrations: Engel (1968, Figures 349–464); Scott (1986, Figure 107); Meagher & Fuhrer
(2006, page 213).
Habitat: Soil in shaded situations in wet forest and rainforest.
Distribution on LHI: Known only from the northern face of Mt Gower and the north-eastern
slope of Mt Lidgbird.
Total distribution: Eastern Australia, New Caledonia and New Zealand.
Discussion: Engel (1968) reported Balantiopsis diplophylla for Lord Howe Island, citing Watts
91c, originally described as B. pusilla Steph. Engel considered the only extant type material of
B. pusilla to be a poorly developed specimen of B. diplophylla (Hook.f. & Taylor) Mitt. at the
extreme end of a series of forms he described, although he did not illustrate this form. Since
then several additional collections of Balantiopsis have been made on Lord Howe Island, and all
match B. pusilla as described by Stephani. Since no other forms have been found on Lord Howe
Island, as one would expect if B. pusilla were only a form of B. diplophylla, there may be no

with up to 100 teeth on apex and ventral margin, teeth small and triangular, comprised of one or two cells,
apical cell triangular, slightly elongated and acute-tipped, and with a single larger spinose-triangular tooth
at the leaf apex; leaf insertion J-shaped, recurved at ventral end, decurrent dorsally, attaining dorsal stem
midline, not attaining the ventral stem midline leaving two or more cortical cell rows leaf-free. Marginal leaf
cells quadrate to short rectangular 7–17 µm long × 8–15 µm wide, long axis parallel or perpendicular to leaf
margin, walls of one to three tiers of marginal cells with continuous golden-brown thickening; medial leaf
cells quadrate to polyhedral, 7–17 µm long × 8–22 µm wide, walls unpigmented, with conspicuous cordate to
bulging trigones and occasional medial thickening; cells in leaf base long rectangular, to 80 µm long × 18 µm
wide, bulging trigones and medial wall thickenings. Cell surfaces smooth. Oil-bodies 2 per cell, ellipsoid,
granular. Underleaves absent. Asexual reproduction absent.
Dioicous. Androecia intercalary on shoots that continue vegetative growth, male branches nodding, ventral-
intercalary and Frullania-type branches not associated with male branches; bracts in 3–6 pairs, imbricate,
closely packed, and tapering, bracts resembling sterile leaves but with a dorsal pouch, antheridia 1 per bract,
stalk biseriate; stem among bracts unornamented. Gynoecia at apices of leafy shoots; bracts ovate-rotund,
larger than subtending leaves but otherwise similar; apex and ventral margin with numerous spinose teeth;
bract cells as for leaf cells; cell surfaces smooth; female bracteole absent. Subfloral innovations produced by
lateral- or ventral-intercalary branching from between the female bracts. Perianth ligulate, to 4000 µm long ×
2500 µm wide at mouth, dorsal and ventral keels not winged, laterally compressed but with a weakly inflated
base, lateral walls plane; labia truncate, each bearing 16–24 spinose teeth. Fig. 4.

Notes: The species currently known as Plagiochila retrospectans, was first described as Jungermannia
retrospectans Nees, but unfortunately this was an illegitimate homonym blocked by Jungermannia retrospectans
Nees ex Spreng. Jungermannia retrospectans Nees ex Spreng. was based on a different type from J. retrospectans
Nees, and today J. retrospectans Nees ex Spreng. is a synonym of Heteroscyphus argutus (Reinw., Blume et
Nees) Schiffn. Twelve years after the publication of Jungermannia retrospectans Nees, Lindenberg (1843)
proposed the species Plagiochila retrospectans Lindenb. Even if Lindenberg had intended to publish Nees’
name under Plagiochila as a new combination (Article 41.4) this could not have been achieved because no
legitimate basionym was available for that combination (Article 6.10). Lindenberg’s name in Plagiochila was
therefore effectively a new name, even though it was based on the same type as Jungermannia retrospectans
Nees. The interpretation by Engel and Merrill (2009), that Lindenberg’s name was a new combination of Nees
ex Sprengl’s name, is incorrect because Lindenberg’s description and syntypes describe and capture the plant
of Nees, not the plant of Nees ex Spreng. Plagiochila retrospectans Lindenb. is therefore the correct citation.
Reference to locations ‘Australia & Brasil’ for the syntypes of Plagiochila retrospectans can be attributed the
fact that the name Nova Hollandia was applied to both Australia and an early Dutch colony near Recife in
Brasil, this confusion was only enhanced by the fact that two different Siebers collected in ‘Nova Hollandia’:
A revision of Australian Plagiochila (Lophocoleinae: Jungermanniopsida)   Telopea 21: 187–380, 2018            211


Franz Wilhelm Sieber in Australia and Friedrich Wilhelm Sieber in Brasil (Anders Hagborg pers. comm. 2015).
Plagiochila retrospectans has not yet been effectively lectotypified. Inoue and Schuster (1971) identified the
Australian plant as the type element but could not locate a specimen of it, while Engel and Merrill (2009)
identified the Australian syntype of J. retrospectans Nees as the holotype of J. retrospectans Nees ex Spreng. A
lectotype for Plagiochila retrospectans Lindenb. is therefore proposed above.
The name Plagiochila squarrosa Steph. n.sp. (nom. herb.) was applied by Stephani to a specimen from
Tasman Peninsula on a rock, Newmans Creek, 2 Feb 1899, W.A. Weymouth 819 (BM!, HO 86208!) which is
P. retrospectans. This name was never published.
Bonner (1962) listed a Petrie specimen gathered in 1898 in hb. G as the type of P. multidentata, but this is in
conflict with the protologue.
Recognition: Plagiochila retrospectans can be recognized by the combination of succubously inserted yet
transversely orientated, ovate to reniform, imbricate leaves with numerous (>80) small triangular teeth
composed of 1 to three cells on the leaf margin, whose cell walls are usually continuously thickened to a degree
greater than the subtending medial leaf cell walls, at the very least on the free external wall; and the presence
of a single larger spinose tooth close to the apical end of the dorsal leaf margin; vegetative branching by lateral-
intercalary mode only; the decurrent wing formed by the dorsal leaf insertion; and the ventral-intercalary

---

thickened, yellow-brown pigmented. Cell surfaces smooth. Oil-bodies 2–6 per cell, ovoid to ellipsoid, finely
botryoidal. Underleaves absent. Asexual reproduction absent.
Dioicous. Androecia intercalary on shoots that continue vegetative growth, in fascicles of up to three branches
produced at the apex of vegetative shoots by Frullania-type branching at the base of the leading male branch;
224           Telopea 21: 187–380, 2018                                                                         Renner


lateral- and ventral-intercalary branches not associated with male branches; bracts in 3–6 pairs, imbricate,
bract-lobe reduced and much smaller than adjacent leaves, margin dentate, with a dorsal pouch, antheridia
1 per bract, stalk biseriate; stem among bracts unornamented. Gynoecia at apices of shoots; bracts broadly
elliptic to triangular-ovate with an ampliate base, to 4000 µm long, larger than subtending leaves; margins
with 60–70 spinose teeth; bract cells as for leaf cells; cell surfaces smooth; female bracteole absent. Subfloral
innovations absent, rarely with a single lateral intercalary innovation produced below the female bracts.
Perianth long cylindrical, to 8000 µm long × 1800 µm wide at mouth, dorsal and ventral keels not winged,
laterally compressed but with a weakly inflated base, lateral walls plane; labia rounded, with around 15 long
spinose teeth each. Fig. 1.
Recognition: Plagiochila gigantea can be recognized by the dendroid shoots with flabellate branching by
Frullania-type mode and monopodial replication of shoot systems resulting in stacking of three or more tiers
of umbrella-like spreading branches. The leaves are elliptic-ovate and bear numerous spinose teeth on their
margins, and the cells of the teeth and leaf margin have thickened, golden-brown-pigmented cell walls.
Plagiochila gigantea could be confused with P. baileyana, but the shoot systems of P. baileyana are procumbent,
not erect, and the leaves are obovate, not elliptic-ovate (Fig. 1).
Plagiochila gigantea could be confused with P. ramosissima which also has a dendroid growth habit, but
vegetative branching in P. ramosissima is by lateral-intercalary mode, not Frullania-type, and the leaves bear
triangular teeth and do not have a border formed by cells with heavily thickened and pigmented cell walls.
Distribution and Ecology: Plagiochila gigantea is endemic to New Zealand, where it is widely distributed
in cool hyperhumid forests throughout the three main islands. Plagiochila gigantea grows on leaf litter, soil,
humus, and decaying logs on the forest floor where it contributes, with several other bryophyte giants, to some
of the tallest, most extensive, and species-rich forest floor liverwort dominated bryophyte communities on
earth. Plagiochila gigantea grows mixed with Schistochila appendiculata and S. nobilis, Lepidozia microphylla,
L. pendulina and L. spinosissima, Trichocolea hatcheri, Plagiochila ramosissima, Heteroscyphus ciliatus, and the
mosses Dendroligotrichum dendroides, Dicranoloma robusta, and D. billardierei.
One specimen of Plagiochila gigantea collected by Max Fleisher in 1903 bears the locality ‘Fern Tree, Tasmania’,
which is on the eastern flank of Mt Wellington near Hobart. This specimen is a copious, large plant from a
readily accessible site close to major centre of population, yet Fleisher’s collection is the only record of P. gigantea
from Australia. A couple of points suggest this record may be in error. Firstly, though potential habitat remains
at Fern Tree and elsewhere in Tasmania, P. gigantea has not been recollected in Tasmania. It is unlikely that
such a large and conspicuous bryophyte would escape detection, or be neglected given its supposed restriction
to New Zealand. Secondly, Fleischer collected around the Derwent River in early April 1903 before his ship
departed for New Zealand, travelling from Hobart to Taranaki, where Fleischer also collected. It is possible
that Fleischer mixed up some of his localities, and I reject P. gigantea from the Australian flora until material
of undeniable provenance is obtained.

stoloniferous section and upper leafy sector, replicated sympodially from basally produced stolons. Leafy shoot
systems monomorphic. Vegetative branching exclusively lateral-intercalary. Teeth on leaves variable, spinose
dentate to triangular. Underleaves absent or vestigial. Subfloral innovations lateral-intercalary. Androecial
branching lateral- or ventral-intercalary. Androecia spicate or lax, intercalary, often in series, male bracts

thread like mats. This habit is reminiscent of Drepanolejeunea which is superficially simi-
lar to R. aneurysmalis. Radula aneurysmalis often grows among other byophytes, particu-
larly R. £lvi/era, R. tasmanica, Heteroscyphus sp. and Frullania spp. Radula aneurysmalis
also grows amongst moss and other hepatics in crevices in rock at high altitudes.
      Recognition: Radula aneurysmalis is distinct in its extremely small size, with shoots
less than 350 pm wide, and in its subequal lobes and lobules.
      Radula aneurysmalis is superficially similar to smaller members of the Lejeuneaceae,
such as Drepanolejeunea and Harpalejeunea , however is immediately identified by its I)
lack of underleaves, 2) production of rhizoids on the ventral surface of the lobule, never on
the stem, 3) the single large oil body per lobe cell, and 4) the dorso-ventrally flattened peri-
anths, that are never inflated.
      Radula aneurysmalis can be confused with R. physoloba, as extensive growth of mi-
crophyllous branches can occur in R. physoloba, particularly when plants of the latter grow
above tree line. However, these branches can always be seen to originate from the large full
sized axes they grow with, and they never produce antheridia or gynoecia. Production of
reproductive organs from microphyllous branches is indicative of R. aneurysmalis. Radula
aneurysmalis can also be distinguished from microphyllous axes of R. physoloba by a
number of features which are summarised in Table I.
      Radula aneUly smalis bears a particular resemblance to R. compacta, best expressed in
the form of the lobules preceding the gynoecia. These two species are separable only by the
persistent microphyllous habit of R. aneurysmalis, and the association of microphyllous
axes with axes of normal stature in R. compacta.
      Notes: While Schuster (1980b) uses the spelling R. aneurismalis, we follow the
spelling presented in Taylor's protologue. Rodway (1916) was of the opinion that R. tas-
manica was a well developed form of R. aneurysmalis. Most likely Rodway was confusing
R. tasmanica with R. physoloba or R. compacta (see under R. tasmanica below) as differ-
ences in the oil-bodies between these two species (see below) clearly indicate that this can-
not be the case, besides which R. tasmanica never produces microphyllous branches. As
pointed out above, this species does bear a marked resemblance to the microphyllous axes
of R. physoloba, and an even closer resemblance, particularly in the form of the lobule on
leaves preceding the production of gynoecia, to R. compacta. Radula aneurysmalis may be
a neotenic derivative of this species, however the affinities of these species need clarifying.

Mountain on Stewart Island, and Secretary Island and Wet Jacket Arm within Fiordland
National Park. At Rocky Mountain, this species is common on the lower trunks of mature
Leptospermum scoparium , within the short Olearia colensoi communities (mutton bird

nity. On Secretary Island R. ratkowskiana was collected from the trunk of Podocarpus hal-
hi in forest at 300 metres altitude. At Wet Jacket Arm this species was collected growing
over bryophytes on a small rock face within Notho{agus menziesii - N. solandri var. cliffor-
tiodes forest canopy on treeline.
      Recognition: The presence of dome shaped papillae over the entire surface of the
lobes is nearly unique within Radula, being shared only with R. ornata E.A.Brown et Pocs
(Brown & Pocs 200 I), and is thus exceptionally di stinctive . The manner in which the labia
of the perianth roll inwards appears similarly unique, as does the occurrence of heteroge-
nous oil-bodies within the same cell. This species is also distinctive in its colour and eco-
logical preference, being a bright green, and, within its known New Zealand range, occur-
ring primarily on the trunks of Dracophy llum longifolium .

oblong, the sides very much parallel, spreading at a wide angle
from the stem. The cells of the leaves are visible under a hand
lens, aligned in about eight neat rows along the length of each
leaf. The underleaves are deeply 4-fid. Sporophytes arise on basal branches from

    T dispar (V) is rather dull olive-brown. It is common on soil in wet sclerophyll
forest; and occasional in other damp habitats. The wedge-shaped leaves are 4-fid on
the main stems but only 3-fid on the branches. The underleaves are 3-fid or 4-fid
on the main stems, but mostly 2-fid on the branches. T patentissima (TV) is very
similar to T centipes, but has 3-fid underleaves. T herzogii (TV) is a minute plant
in which the leaves and underleaves are reduced to a pair of long, spine-like lobes.
It is quite common in tree-fern gullies in wet forest and rainforest, creeping
through other bryophytes, but it is probably commonly overlooked because of its
size.

Similar species: Lepidozia glaucophylla, Leptophyllopsis laxa

Chiloecyphus Lophocoleaceae
[most Lophocolea species of Scott ( 1985) belong to this genus]
In the field the differences between this genus and Heteroscyphus are not easily defined.
In Chiloscyphus at least one leaf in each pair is not joined to the corresponding
underleaf, but in Heteroscyphus both leaves are usually joined.

Similar species: *Geocalyx caledonicus, Heteroscyphus spp., Lethocolea pansa, Jungermannia
spp., *Pedinophyllum monoicum, Plagiochila spp.

C. latifoliue Lophocoleaceae                                                    WSTVAN
The shoots of this spec1es (for merly Lophocolea
bidentata) are green to straw-coloured, forming loose wefts
often creeping through other bryophytes in grasslands and
grassy understoreys. The leaves have two long, narrow
spines at the leaf apex, often curved away from each other. The
dorsal margin is more or less straight, but the ventral margin is
distinctly rounded. The underleaves are deeply bifid to
beyond half-way, often with long extra teeth.
     C. biciliatus (TV), a mainly forest species, has leaves
with shorter apical spines and curved margins.

C. muricatue Lophocoleaceae
                                                                                  STVAN
This is a common but overlooked species in wet forests, where
it grows on bark, rotting wood, and sometimes leaves and fern
fronds. The leaves are mostly bilobed and covered in spike-
like papillae on the dorsal leaf surface, and there are scattered
papillae on the ventral surface. The leaves thus resemble
minute, rough tongues. The colour is usually deep green, with        C. muricatus {leaf in
paler new growth. The dorsal side of the stem is hidden.                 dorsal view}
C. echinellus (TV) also has papillose leaves, but the stem is
visible between the leaves and is also papillose, and the leaf
margins are irregularly toothed.

---

This distinctive species is much more common than was once
thought, but seems never to form large colonies. It grows in fern



                                                                                  fr
gullies and rainforest, where the shoots (2-3 mm wide) meander
over soil or rotting wood. The leaves are almost rectangular, with
almost parallel sides and a rounded apex that always carries two
to several small teeth. The underleaves are rather small, with two
widely spreading fobes that usually also have a tooth on each side.

around the stem, forming in effect one continuous leaf. The
colour is generally yellow-brown, and the leaves tend to be
curved down, forming a caterpillar-like shoot.

 This Fommon species grows mainly on soil and rotting logs in wet

H. conjugatue Lophocoleaceae                                                         TV
This species is recognised by the more or less upright shoots
with hooded tips.The leaves are concave so that the shoots appear
to be almost tubular, and the leaf margins are entire, except for
occasional teeth on the dorsal margin near the leaf base (invisible
in the field). The underleaves are also concave and entire and
are not much smaller than the leaves.
    H circumdentatus (T) is similar in appearance in the field,         H. conjugatus
but the leaves and underleaves are toothed all around.
    H cymbaliferus (TV) - Tetracymbaliella cymbalifera of Scott (1985) - is
remark�ble in having semicircular sacs on leaves and lobes. It is a very small species,
and the leaves are curled around the stem so that the structure is rather hard to see.

H. planiuecu/ue; Lophocoleaceae                                                     STVN




                                                                 uO
One of the few aquatic Geocalycaceae in Australia, this
species grows on rocks in streams, from sea level to the Alps.
The dark green shoots are 20 to 80 mm long and the leaves
appear to be roughly circular, although clearly broader than
long when stripped from- the stem. The underleaves are
characteristically large and oval with a deep apical notch
and usually carry two or four small teeth, especially near the base. The apical lobes
often curve inward like pincers, but may be eroded away.
    H gunnianus (TV) is very similar but usually much smaller and more yellowish
green. The underleaves are entire or have an extra tooth at the centre of the margin or
above, not near the base. This difference, however, is impossible to detect in the field.
It grows in much the same habitat as H planiusculus, although reportedly often farther
out of the water.

      A 80. Hrterosqphus conjugatus (xl)


80. Heterosqphus conjugatus is a robust golden-brown species which can
    form large patches, sometimes 50-60 cm across, on the forest floor.
    The stems are sparingly branched and the edges of the two lateral
    rows of leaves often roll towards each other resulting in large worm-
    like shoots.

81. Heteroscyphus cyrnbal$ms forms compact clumps of small, pale yellow-
    green shoots on tree trunks or logs. The underleaf has a very
    distinctive hamrner-head shape.

82. Heterosqphus decipiens has pale-coloured leaves with entire rnargins
    and a rounded tip. It grows on logs or soil, usually in wcll-lit
    situations.

83. Heterosqphus sinuosus is a large species with undulate leaves and
    underleaves. It grows on logs and rocks.

                                                                                                                                                                                   Leaves divided into 4 long narrow lobes; lobes parallel to stem ................................. 8
                                                                                                                                                                               8   Leaf lobes spine-like, bent in centre; leaves succubous ........... Psiloclada clandestina
                                                                                                                                                                                   Leaf lobes narrowly to widely triangular; leaves ± transverse ........................... Kurzia
                                                                                                                                                                               9   Underleaves always joined to leaves on both sides, usually
                                                                                                                                                                                    strongly .............................................................................................. Heteroscyphus
                                                                                                                                                                                   Underleaves joined to leaves on 1 side only, or not joined at all .............................. 10

                                                                                                                                                                               10 Leaves with irregular fragile teeth on margin, often broken off,
                                                                                                                                                                                    giving leaves a ragged appearance; cuticle with a distinct
                                                                                                                                                                                    rainbow sheen .......................................................................... Leptophyllopsis laxa
                                                                                                                                                                                  Leaves without such marginal teeth; cuticle without a distinct rainbow sheen ......... 11
                                                                                                                                                                               11 Leaves ± transverse, 4-lobed to almost half way; stolons present;
                                                                                                                                                                                    rare plant of subalpine woodland ............................... Pseudocephalozia paludicola
                                                                                                                                                                                  Leaves clearly succubous, not deeply 4-lobed; stolons not present .......................... 12
                                                                                                                                                                               12 Sporophyte developing in perianth on short lateral branch;
                                                                                                                                                                                    underleaves usually joined to leaves on 1 side, sometimes
                                                                                                                                                                                    narrowly; leaves ± circular to tongue-shaped ...................................... Chiloscyphus
                                                                                                                                                                                  Sporophyte developing in marsupium on short branch on underside
                                                                                                                                                                                    of stem; underleaves clearly not joined to leaves; leaves various ......................... 13
                                                                                                                                                                               13 Leaves ± oblong, deeply lobed at apex; underleaves divided to
                                                                                                                                                                                    the base into 2 diverging lobes* ............................................. Geocalyx caledonicus
                                                                                                                                                                                  Leaves ± triangular-ovate, entire or very shallowly lobed at apex;
                                                                                                                                                                                    underleaves almost circular, shallowly notched at apex .................. Saccogynidium

                                                                                                                                                                               * Species of Lophozia, a genus not yet formally reported for Victoria but undoubtedly
                                                                                                                                                                                  present here, could key out at couplet 13.

WIKIPEDIA  (1) 
Heteroscyphus is a genus of liverworts in the family Lophocoleaceae. 87 species was accepted in this worldwide group in 2019.
